rows.name: Visual hierarchy
rows.one_line: A layout should make the order in which things are meant to be read visible before any of them is read.
rows.plain_gloss: Before someone reads a single word, the page has already told them what to look at first. If it hasn't, they pick for themselves — and they usually pick wrong.
rows.confidence_note: Long-standing studio and editorial practice with no single origin; it is a way of describing what scale, weight, space and position do together rather than a finding of its own.
rows.common_misuse: Treated as 'make the important thing big', which produces three big things and therefore no hierarchy at all. Hierarchy is a ranking, and a ranking needs things below the top.
rows.limits: It assumes the designer knows what the reader wants first. On a screen serving two readers with different questions — a bill read by a customer and by a call handler — there is no single correct order, and the honest answer is two layouts or an explicit compromise.

rows.name: Contrast (visual weight)
rows.one_line: Difference is what makes an element noticeable; an element that differs from its neighbours in nothing will not be seen as separate from them.
rows.plain_gloss: Things stand out by being different from what is around them, not by being loud. A heavy word among light ones is louder than a heavy word among heavy ones.
rows.confidence_note: Craft vocabulary rather than a sourced claim. It is the working half of visual hierarchy and is taught as technique, not as evidence.
rows.common_misuse: Reached for as a synonym for colour contrast, so a student writes 'good contrast' about a layout and means the text passes a ratio check. They are different arguments and only one of them is measurable.
rows.limits: Contrast is relative to context, so it cannot be specified once for a design system and applied everywhere. The same treatment that separates a heading on a sparse page disappears on a dense one.

rows.name: Scale
rows.one_line: Relative size is the fastest signal of importance available on a screen, and it is read before shape, colour or wording.
rows.plain_gloss: Size is the first thing anyone notices, so whatever you set biggest is the thing you have decided matters — whether or not that is what you meant.
rows.confidence_note: Studio practice. The related empirical work concerns legibility at a given size, which is a different claim from the one made here about relative size and importance.
rows.common_misuse: Used to build a type scale with seven steps, five of which are never distinguishable in use. A scale earns a step only when a reader can tell it from the step below.
rows.limits: Scale competes with position: something small at the top of a page can outrank something large below the fold, so size cannot be reasoned about apart from where it sits.

rows.name: Proximity
rows.one_line: Elements placed close together are perceived as belonging together, and the perception happens before any label is read.
rows.plain_gloss: Put two things near each other and people assume they go together. Space does the grouping whether you meant it to or not — which is why a label drifting towards the wrong field is read as belonging to it.
rows.origin: Max Wertheimer, 'Laws of Organization in Perceptual Forms', 1923 (Ellis translation, 1938)
rows.confidence_note: Stated in Wertheimer's 1923 paper as the Factor of Proximity; the cited page carries the translated text itself rather than a description of it.
rows.common_misuse: Applied as 'add space between sections' while the spacing inside a section stays the same, so the grouping is announced and then contradicted. The gap within must be smaller than the gap between, and usually is not.
rows.limits: Proximity is a grouping cue, not a hierarchy cue: it says these things belong together, and says nothing about which of them matters. It also loses to a strong border or a fill, which can group elements that are far apart.

rows.name: Similarity
rows.one_line: Elements that share an appearance are perceived as a set, even when they are separated in space.
rows.plain_gloss: Anything that looks the same gets read as the same kind of thing. Style two unrelated items alike and people will assume they do the same job.
rows.origin: Max Wertheimer, 'Laws of Organization in Perceptual Forms', 1923 (Ellis translation, 1938)
rows.confidence_note: Stated in Wertheimer's 1923 paper as the Factor of Similarity, on the same page as proximity; both are quoted there in the translated text.
rows.common_misuse: Turned into a licence to style every clickable thing identically, so a destructive action and a harmless one become members of the same visible set and are chosen with the same care.
rows.limits: Similarity and proximity can be made to disagree, and when they do the outcome depends on how strong each cue is — which the principle does not predict. It is a description of grouping, not a rule for resolving conflicts between groupings.

rows.name: Figure and ground
rows.one_line: Perception separates a scene into a shape being attended to and a background it sits on, and only one of them can be the figure at a time.
rows.plain_gloss: Your eye picks one thing to be the object and treats everything else as the backdrop. It cannot do both at once, so if the design does not settle which is which, the reader will — and it may not go your way.
rows.confidence_note: The origin is named and datable, but the 1915 thesis is in Danish and no page could be found that states the claim rather than summarising it, so this is not marked documented. That gap is the point of the marker, not a defect in the record.
rows.common_misuse: Read as a curiosity about ambiguous vases rather than as the reason a modal with a weak overlay fails: if the background is still legible, it is still competing to be the figure.
rows.limits: It describes what perception does, not what a design should do, and it says nothing about which of two candidates will win. A low-contrast overlay and a heavy one both obey it.

rows.name: Alignment
rows.one_line: Shared edges create an implied line, and that line does structural work that no visible rule or border has to do.
rows.plain_gloss: When things line up, the eye draws an invisible edge between them and reads them as connected. You get a structure without adding a single line to the page.
rows.confidence_note: Typographic and layout craft with no single citable origin. It is the practical reason a grid is worth having, and it is taught by demonstration.
rows.common_misuse: Everything centred, which produces two ragged edges and no line at all — then a border is added to supply the structure that the alignment was supposed to provide.
rows.limits: An implied line is weaker than a real one and will not survive a crowded page or a narrow viewport, so alignment alone is not enough where a genuine boundary is needed.

rows.name: White space
rows.one_line: Empty area is a working part of a layout: it separates, groups and paces, and removing it removes those functions.
rows.plain_gloss: The gaps are doing a job. Space is not the bit left over after the content is placed — it is what tells someone where one thing ends and the next begins.
rows.confidence_note: Long-standing print and studio practice. The general claim is craft; the specific figures people attach to it — golden gaps, fixed ratios — are not sourced and are not repeated here.
rows.common_misuse: Defended as 'it needs to breathe' while the space is distributed evenly, which groups nothing. Uniform space is the same as no space as far as grouping is concerned.
rows.limits: Space is expensive on a small screen and in print, and on a dense screen — a timetable, a bill — the honest solution is often rules and tints rather than more air.

rows.name: Measure (line length)
rows.one_line: Line length affects the ease of returning from the end of one line to the start of the next, and screen type is often set far wider than it is set in print.
rows.plain_gloss: If a line runs too long, your eye loses its place coming back to the left. Most bad-looking screen text is not the wrong font — it is a line that runs the full width of a laptop.
rows.origin: Commonly attributed to Robert Bringhurst, 'The Elements of Typographic Style', 1992; the practice is considerably older
rows.confidence_note: The familiar 45-75 character range is stated in the typographic literature as craft judgement rather than as the result of a named experiment, so it is recorded as traditional. No study is cited here because none was verified.
rows.common_misuse: The character range is quoted as though it were a measured threshold and then applied to everything, including captions, table cells and buttons, where it has no bearing at all.
rows.limits: The range is stated for continuous prose in a Latin script. It does not transfer to short text, to tabular content, or to scripts with different word lengths and no spaces, and the acceptable range widens as line height increases.

rows.name: Line height
rows.one_line: The space between lines and the length of the lines have to be decided together, because each changes how much of the other a reader can tolerate.
rows.plain_gloss: Leading and line length are one decision, not two. Long lines need more space between them; tight lines need to be shorter. Setting one without the other is how text ends up hard to read for no obvious reason.
rows.confidence_note: Typographic craft. It is taught as a relationship to be judged by eye against the actual text, not as a number, and no source is claimed for a number.
rows.common_misuse: A single line-height set once in a design system and applied to headings, body text and captions alike, so headings gap and captions crowd.
rows.limits: Optimal spacing depends on the typeface's x-height and on the script, so a value that works for one face is not portable to another. Accessibility requirements set a floor here but do not set the right value.

rows.name: Contrast (minimum)
rows.one_line: Text and images of text must reach a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against their background, or 3:1 for large-scale text.
rows.plain_gloss: There is an actual number for whether text is dark enough against its background, and you can check it. It is the one part of colour that is not a matter of taste.
rows.origin: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Level AA)
rows.confidence_note: The cited W3C page states the criterion and both thresholds in its normative text, including the definition of large-scale text as 18 point or 14 point bold.
rows.common_misuse: Checked once on the design's main text and declared passed, while placeholder text, disabled states, text over photographs and the focus indicator — the places it actually fails — are never measured.
rows.limits: It is a floor, not a target, and it is a ratio between two specific colours. It says nothing about whether a palette is legible in sunlight, whether two adjacent hues are distinguishable, or whether the type is large enough to read.

rows.name: Use of colour
rows.one_line: Colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response or distinguishing an element.
rows.plain_gloss: If the only thing telling someone that a field is wrong is that it turned red, then for a lot of people nothing has told them. Colour always needs a second signal carrying the same message.
rows.origin: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, Success Criterion 1.4.1 (Level A)
rows.confidence_note: The cited W3C page states the criterion in its normative text; the wording quoted in this record is that text rather than a paraphrase of it.
rows.common_misuse: Satisfied by adding an icon that is itself only distinguishable by colour, or by adding text that appears somewhere else on the page rather than where the colour was doing the work.
rows.limits: It requires a second cue but does not say the second cue must be equally noticeable, so a design can satisfy the criterion with a signal nobody sees. Passing here is not the same as the message getting through.

rows.name: Target size (minimum)
rows.one_line: The target for a pointer input should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, subject to stated exceptions for spacing, equivalents, inline targets and essential cases.
rows.plain_gloss: A tap target has a minimum size, and it is bigger than the icon you can see. What matters is the area that responds to a finger, not how large the symbol looks.
rows.origin: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Level AA)
rows.confidence_note: The cited W3C page states the 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum and enumerates the five exceptions — spacing, equivalent, inline, user agent control and essential — which this record summarises rather than reproduces.
rows.common_misuse: The visible icon is measured instead of the hit area, so a design passes on paper and fails in the hand; or the spacing exception is invoked without ever checking the 24-pixel circle it actually specifies.
rows.limits: It is a minimum for pointer input, not a recommendation, and 24 pixels is smaller than most platform guidance suggests. It also says nothing about where the target sits — a large target at the top of a tall phone is still hard to reach.

rows.name: Focus order
rows.one_line: Where a page can be navigated sequentially and that sequence affects meaning or operation, focusable components must receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.
rows.plain_gloss: Tabbing through a page walks it in a set order. If that order jumps around, someone using a keyboard is being handed the screen shuffled, and the layout you designed is not the one they get.
rows.origin: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, Success Criterion 2.4.3 (Level A)
rows.confidence_note: The cited W3C page states the criterion in its normative text, including the condition that the sequence must affect meaning or operation for the criterion to apply.
rows.common_misuse: Confused with the visual order, so a student rearranges a layout with CSS and assumes the focus order followed. It follows the source, and the two silently diverge the moment a column is reordered.
rows.limits: It requires an order that preserves meaning, not the order the designer imagined, and it says nothing about whether that order is efficient. A logical sequence through forty fields is still forty fields.

rows.name: Reflow
rows.one_line: Content must be presentable without loss of information or functionality and without two-dimensional scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels, with stated exceptions.
rows.plain_gloss: Zoom a page right in and it has to reorganise itself into one column, without hiding anything and without making you scroll sideways to read a sentence. Shrinking the layout does not count.
rows.origin: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Level AA)
rows.confidence_note: The cited W3C page states the criterion, both measurements — 320 CSS pixels wide for vertically scrolling content and 256 for horizontally scrolling content — and the exception for content requiring two-dimensional layout.
rows.common_misuse: Treated as a mobile-layout requirement and tested by resizing a browser window, when the case it exists for is a desktop page at high zoom, where fixed toolbars and sticky headers eat the viewport.
rows.limits: The exception for content that genuinely needs two dimensions — tables, maps, diagrams — is broad, and it is routinely claimed for layouts that could reflow. The criterion cannot decide that for you.

rows.name: Error identification
rows.one_line: If an input error is automatically detected, the item in error must be identified and the error described to the user in text.
rows.plain_gloss: When something goes wrong in a form, the person has to be told which field it was and what was wrong with it, in words. A red outline says something is wrong and not what.
rows.origin: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, Success Criterion 3.3.1 (Level A)
rows.confidence_note: The cited W3C page states the criterion in its normative text and makes explicit that the description must be in text and must identify the item in error.
rows.common_misuse: Satisfied with a summary at the top of the form saying that errors were found, leaving the reader to hunt for which field and why. Identification means the field, and description means the reason.
rows.limits: It covers errors the system detects. An answer that is wrong but well-formed — the right format, the wrong date — is outside it entirely, and that is the error that costs people most.

rows.name: Consistency
rows.one_line: The same thing should look and behave the same way throughout a design, so that what is learned in one place transfers to the next.
rows.plain_gloss: Once someone works out what a thing does, they should not have to work it out again two screens later. Every unexplained variation is a small re-learning cost you have charged them.
rows.confidence_note: Long-standing practice underpinning design systems and platform guidelines; it is a design commitment rather than a finding, and no single source is claimed.
rows.common_misuse: Used to defend keeping something bad because it is already everywhere, or applied so uniformly that a dangerous action becomes indistinguishable from a safe one. Consistency is a means, and it can be bought too dearly.
rows.limits: Internal consistency and consistency with the platform can conflict, and one must give way. It also cannot tell you which of two conventions to standardise on — only that standardising has value.

rows.name: Mapping
rows.one_line: A control laid out to correspond to what it affects is faster to use and less error-prone than one that must be learned by label.
rows.plain_gloss: If the switches sit in the same arrangement as the things they turn on, nobody has to remember which is which. Get that correspondence wrong and no amount of labelling fully fixes it.
rows.origin: Named as 'natural mapping' by Donald Norman, 'The Design of Everyday Things', 1988; the underlying stimulus-response compatibility experiments are Fitts and Seeger, 1953
rows.confidence_note: The cited page states and argues the claim in its own right rather than summarising Norman, and names the underlying experiment — Fitts and Seeger, 'S-R compatibility', Journal of Experimental Psychology 46(3), 1953. Note this is the same Fitts as the law on the Stairwell and a different piece of work.
rows.common_misuse: Reduced to 'use a familiar icon', which is a recognition argument, not a mapping one. Mapping is about the spatial or ordinal correspondence between the control and the effect, not about what the control depicts.
rows.limits: It requires an effect with a structure worth corresponding to. Much of a screen has no such structure — there is no natural arrangement for save, share and delete — and forcing one produces arbitrary layouts defended as intuitive.

rows.name: Progressive disclosure
rows.one_line: Show the small set of options most people need, and keep the rest reachable rather than absent, so the common case stays simple without removing the uncommon one.
rows.plain_gloss: Put the few things nearly everyone wants up front and tuck the rest behind one more step. The point is not to hide features — it is that the person who needs the rare one can still get to it.
rows.confidence_note: Established interaction practice described in many places; no single origin was verified for the claim as it is stated here, so it is recorded as traditional rather than attributed.
rows.common_misuse: Used to justify hiding things the user needs every time, so the second step becomes part of the common path and the disclosure has added work rather than removed it.
rows.limits: It depends on knowing which case is common, which is a research question, not a design one. Where usage is genuinely split, disclosure penalises half the users and a different structure is needed.

rows.name: The three-click rule
rows.one_line: The claim that anything on a site must be reachable within three clicks or users will give up. Repeated constantly and not supported as a threshold.
rows.plain_gloss: You will hear that everything has to be three clicks away. It isn't true — people keep going as long as each step feels like progress. What makes them quit is not knowing whether they are getting closer.
rows.origin: Widely repeated in web design writing from the late 1990s onward; no origin study has ever been produced for it
rows.confidence_note: Tested by Joshua Porter for User Interface Engineering in 2003 across 44 users and 620 tasks, analysing over 8,000 clicks: quitting was no more likely after three clicks than after twelve, and click count did not correlate with success or satisfaction. Marked folk rather than documented because the sourced finding is against the rule, not for it, and the brief reserves source_url for claims the source supports.
rows.common_misuse: Used to justify flattening navigation into a menu of sixty items, which trades three honest steps for one impossible choice — and then cited as a rule in a portfolio rationale, where it is the citation rather than the layout that fails.
rows.limits: Rejecting the threshold does not mean click count is free. The finding is that certainty of progress matters more than the number of steps, so it replaces a countable target with a judgement, which is harder to design against and harder to mark.

known_gaps: Nine rows are marked documented and eleven are not. That ratio is the honest state of this subject: the accessibility half has a normative specification behind it and the visual half is craft, and no amount of searching turns craft into a citation.

figure-ground has a named, datable origin (Rubin, 1915) and is still marked traditional, because the thesis is in Danish and every findable page about it summarises rather than states it. It is the clearest example in the set of the difference between knowing where a claim came from and being able to cite it.

measure and line-height are the two rows most likely to be challenged. Both are taught with numbers (the 45-75 character range, a leading ratio) and neither number is sourced here. They are recorded as craft because that is what they are; if a tutor wants a number defended in week 4, that defence does not yet exist in this file.

Only one folk row was found worth returning. There are more candidates in circulation - the fold, users not scrolling, colour psychology - but each needs its counter-evidence verified before it can be entered, and that work was not done here.
weeks[] is filled on every row against the lecture plan in screen-design-plan.html. If that plan moves, this field is stale and nothing in the schema will say so.

No row carries a working bench in the Stairwell's sense - two real interfaces for one task. Until screens.json exists there is nothing to point at, which is the same dependency that blocks y-cases.json.

dropped.name: Repetition
dropped.why: Overlaps consistency, which is returned in the ucd family and is the more useful framing at Level 4 because it extends to behaviour and not only to appearance. Returning both would have spent two of twenty slots on one idea.

dropped.name: The optical centre
dropped.why: A craft adjustment rather than a principle: it is real, it is applied by eye, and it could not be stated in one line without either inventing a ratio or reducing to 'a bit above the middle'. Neither is markable.

dropped.name: Chunking
dropped.why: Inseparable from Miller at the level this dataset states things, and Miller is on the Stairwell already, marked folk. Entering chunking here would produce a row that either duplicates that record or quietly contradicts its marker.

dropped.name: Redundancy of coding
dropped.why: As it would be stated for Level 4 it is use-of-colour with a wider scope, and use-of-colour is returned with a normative source behind it. The general version has no source and would have been the weaker of two near-identical rows.

dropped.name: Focus visible (SC 2.4.7)
dropped.why: Verified and sourceable, and dropped only for room: it sits in week 9 alongside focus-order, target-size and reflow, and four accessibility rows in one week is more than that week can teach. This is the first candidate to reinstate if the cap is ever raised.
